impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that patent claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's headache patents, which had been found willfully infringed by Eli Lilly. The court held that claims directed to humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache satisfied written description and enablement requirements, reinstating a jury verdict of willful infringement. This case has significant implications for the CGRP migraine drug market worth billions of dollars annually.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens the enforceability of genus claims in the biopharmaceutical space, particularly for antibody patents where the specification discloses known methods for making and humanizing antibodies, benefiting patent holders with broad therapeutic claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates greater exposure for pharmaceutical companies developing competing antibody therapies, as broad method-of-treatment claims covering a class of antibodies may be harder to invalidate under § 112.

impacts.caseName: The Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions using an emulator and comparing function calls to a model are directed to an abstract idea under Alice step one, and whether the district court erred in allowing damages based on foreign sales.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict for Columbia University against Norton (Gen Digital), holding that the asserted cybersecurity patent claims are abstract at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign sales were improperly awarded, reinforcing the presumption against extraterritorial application of patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies with stronger defenses against broad software patent claims, particularly in cybersecurity, and limits patent damages exposure for products sold outside the United States.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and patent holders asserting software-related patents face heightened § 101 eligibility risks, and cannot rely on worldwide sales as a damages base without establishing a domestic nexus.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to support the jury's finding that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether information that is generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury's finding of trade secret misappropriation for four asserted trade secrets related to cosmetic penile implants, holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove the information qualified as protectable trade secrets under California law because the information was generally known. The court also reversed the patent invalidity finding, since the alleged inventive contribution was based on the same generally known ideas. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against trade secret claims benefit from a reinforced standard requiring plaintiffs to clearly establish that asserted trade secrets are not generally known in the relevant industry, providing a stronger evidentiary bar for trade secret plaintiffs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face heightened scrutiny at trial to demonstrate that each asserted secret is not generally known, and cannot rely on broadly defined trade secrets without specific evidence of secrecy.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit, where Insulet had notice of potential misappropriation years before filing.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict finding trade secret misappropriation by EOFlow in the development of a competing insulin patch pump, holding that Insulet's DTSA claim was time-barred. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the misappropriation more than three years before filing suit, based on its awareness that former employees had shared proprietary information with EOFlow. This decision vacated the damages award and permanent injunction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from strict enforcement of the DTSA's three-year statute of limitations, particularly where the plaintiff had early knowledge of the alleged misappropriation.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon discovering potential misappropriation or risk losing their claims entirely, even where the full scope of misappropriation was not immediately apparent.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting summary judgment of noninfringement based on extraterritoriality and in striking a damages expert's theories for failure to comply with disclosure requirements.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially reversed summary judgment of noninfringement for Intel, finding that VLSI raised genuine issues of material fact regarding whether Intel's multicore processor selection methods infringed the '836 patent. The court reversed the extraterritoriality ruling but affirmed the district court's striking of certain damages theories for inadequate disclosure, and remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders asserting claims against semiconductor and processor companies benefit from the court's narrower application of extraterritoriality defenses where the accused method has a domestic component.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued patent litigation exposure for processor architectures, and the decision reinforces that damages experts must comply strictly with disclosure requirements or risk exclusion.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data using passive data collection devices on farming equipment are patent-ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in finding the case was not exceptional under § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents were directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under § 101, finding that the claims merely automate conventional data gathering and processing. The court vacated and remanded the district court's finding that the case was not exceptional, suggesting that the weakness of the patent claims may warrant attorneys' fees for the defendant.
impacts.positiveImplications: Agtech and IoT companies defending against broad data-collection patent assertions benefit from continued Federal Circuit skepticism of claims that merely automate conventional processes using generic technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in precision agriculture and IoT data systems face significant § 101 eligibility hurdles, and may face exceptional case findings and fee-shifting for asserting weak patents.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a verdict form that asked a single question on infringement covering all asserted patents, without specifying which patent was infringed, requires vacatur and a new trial on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated an $11.5 million patent infringement verdict against ecobee because the verdict form improperly combined all four asserted patents into a single infringement question, making it impossible to determine which patents the jury found infringed. The court remanded for a new trial on infringement and damages, while also vacating and remanding on § 101 eligibility for one patent and affirming eligibility for others.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the requirement that verdict forms in multi-patent cases must separately identify which patents are infringed, providing grounds to challenge overbroad jury verdicts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs asserting multiple patents must ensure verdict forms require patent-by-patent findings, or risk vacatur of favorable jury verdicts and costly retrials.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the damages verdict and expert testimony were properly upheld.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility, finding that some claims related to non-uniform constellation designs for digital communications required further analysis under Alice, while affirming eligibility for other claims and upholding the jury's infringement and damages findings against LG Electronics. The case involves standards-essential technology for digital broadcasting.
impacts.positiveImplications: Standards-essential patent holders benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for claims that incorporate specific technical improvements to communication systems, and from upheld damages verdicts and expert testimony methodologies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology implementers face continued exposure to infringement claims from patents covering communication standards, and certain eligibility challenges may require deeper factual analysis rather than summary disposition.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation and sale of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement features violated Section 337 by infringing Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing and selling Apple Watches that infringed Masimo's patents on wearable blood oxygen measurement devices, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models. The court found no error in the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the wearable health technology space are strengthened by this affirmance, demonstrating that the ITC remains an effective forum for enforcing patents against major technology companies importing infringing products.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies importing products with patented health-monitoring features face significant supply chain disruption from ITC exclusion orders, potentially requiring product redesigns or licensing agreements.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge for purposes of summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires the prior art sale to expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify to matters beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment and that the on-sale bar does not require the prior art sale to expressly disclose the sold device's functionality. The court also ruled that source code constitutes non-hearsay computer commands admissible as evidence.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants challenging patent validity benefit from broader admissibility of 30(b)(6) testimony and source code evidence, and from a confirmed broad reading of the on-sale bar that does not require public disclosure of functionality in prior sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face greater invalidity risk when prior art products were commercially sold before the critical date, even if the product's infringing functionality was not publicly known or disclosed at the time of sale.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue third parties for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish constitutional standing to bring an infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who grants an exclusive license to a third party but retains the right to independently sue for infringement possesses sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing. The court found the retained right to sue was not illusory given the licensing agreement's structure.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring license agreements can retain standing to enforce patents against infringers by carefully retaining the right to sue, even while granting broad exclusive commercial licenses to licensees.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers face broader exposure to patent suits from both licensors and licensees, as patent owners with retained enforcement rights can independently pursue litigation.

impacts.caseName: Actelion Pharmaceuticals Ltd v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the claim term 'a pH of 13 or higher' in a pharmaceutical composition patent refers to pH measured at the temperature standard in the field, and whether the patent holder was barred from asserting infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding of no literal infringement and no infringement under the doctrine of equivalents for Actelion's epoprostenol formulation patents asserted against Mylan's generic drug ANDA. The court agreed that pH claim terms must be interpreted at the standard temperature in the field, which Mylan's formulation did not meet, and that Actelion was barred from asserting equivalents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies benefit from precise claim construction of measurable parameters like pH, which can defeat infringement allegations when the accused product's measurements differ under standard conditions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies may find it harder to enforce patents with measurable parameter limitations against generic competitors when claims are construed at field-standard measurement conditions.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the deadline to seek a mandatory stay of its original district court declaratory judgment action under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) may obtain a mandatory stay by filing a new declaratory judgment action and timely seeking a stay of that refiled action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay under § 1659(a)(2) by dismissing its original declaratory judgment action and refiling a new one. The court found this would undermine the statutory scheme designed to coordinate parallel ITC and district court proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: ITC complainants (typically patent holders) benefit from the assurance that respondents cannot manipulate the mandatory stay mechanism by strategically dismissing and refiling district court actions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies facing parallel ITC and district court patent proceedings must strictly comply with the 30-day deadline for seeking a mandatory stay or lose the right to one, even through creative procedural maneuvering.

impacts.caseName: National Veterans Legal Services Program v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's approval of a $125 million settlement in a nationwide class action alleging that the federal judiciary charged excessive PACER fees beyond the statutory authorization. The court upheld the settlement, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to the nonprofit class representatives, finding no abuse of discretion.
impacts.positiveImplications: The settlement provides reimbursement to hundreds of thousands of PACER users, including businesses and law firms, and establishes boundaries on the government's ability to use court access fees for unrelated purposes.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTAB's obviousness determination must be vacated where the Board failed to adequately explain its reasoning regarding specific claim limitations, and whether a non-party to underlying litigation may file IPR petitions on behalf of time-barred parties.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent, finding that the Board failed to adequately explain its analysis regarding specific dependent claim limitations. The court declined to review the challenge to the Board's refusal to terminate the IPR based on allegations that Qualcomm filed as a proxy for time-barred Roambee, and remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the requirement that the PTAB must provide adequate explanations for obviousness findings, particularly regarding specific claim limitations, providing a basis for vacatur when reasoning is insufficient.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies using IPR proceedings to challenge competitor patents may face renewed scrutiny of their petitions, though the court declined to address the proxy-filing issue substantively.
